title: REA confident in the power of AI for growth
full_text:
Digital real estate company REA Group is confident the artificial intelligence revolution is taking shape in a way that will favour greater use of its technologies in the property and financial world.
After his latest visit to Silicon Valley, chief executive Cameron McIntyre says conditions are stabilising and opportunities are opening up for companies to adopt AI as they roll out new products.
AI is emerging as one of the drivers of REA as it invests in tools for agents and consumers.
“I’d say from last year to this year it feels like things are stabilising,” he said. “It feels like there’s more thoughtfulness and strategy around the way in which AI has been deployed.
“It felt like there’s more alignment between tech companies and ourselves, just in terms of the journey that they’re on and the journey that we’re on.” Although the company is in a tougher environment after the Albanese government’s property tax changes and rising interest rates, Mr McIntyre believes it has the right mix to advance.
“It felt like there’s lots of opportunities for us as a business and we talk about metabolising AI through the company,” he said. “What that means is how does AI get applied to products? How does it get applied the way we work? How does it apply to the way that we design and develop products?” Amid the AI hype that has infected global markets, the REA chief says real advances are being made on the ground.
“The way we’re thinking about our metabolisation and the way others are, it’s very much aligned, and last year it just felt more like the Wild West,” he said.
“Nothing had landed, and things were landing all over the place, whereas this year it actually felt like we were all in a good spot.” Mr McIntyre said REA already uses AI-driven and agentic tools. “They’re starting to power search and the consumer experience,” he said. For agents and mortgage brokers, it is eliminating “friction points” to drive better decisions.
“Our brokers use their AI agents more than they use email,” he said, noting the systems also lift quality and help lock down customers amid the tough market.
REA data is being used to work out “listing propensity” and bring listings forward.
Property hunters can also use the tools to track down suitable properties and customise their long-term experience.
However, the market remains tough with REA saying that listing volumes would be down in the low single-digit range over this financial year.
Mr McIntyre said there was a two-speed property market. Listing volumes have come off in Sydney and Melbourne, but more stock was coming in Adelaide, Perth and Brisbane, where supply had been constrained.
“We just need to see the top of the interest rate cycle,” he said. “Once we see the top of the interest rate cycle, it gives people more confidence to transact.” Meanwhile the slower market is increasing the time taken to sell a home, with more stock now displayed. Mr McIntyre noted the shift to more depth products as they are more compelling for vendors in the challenged market.
REA, in which News Corporation, publisher of The Australian, has a majority interest, is also diversified beyond Australia.
It last month snapped up a 35 per cent stake in Ireland and Northern Ireland’s largest property website Distilled for $409m. The listed company last year also took a 61.5 per cent stake in Planitar Inc., the Canadian company behind iGUIDE, which has systems that produce 3D tours. It launched in Australia earlier this year and there are about 600 cameras now in the market.
